```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6)
```

Do two groups, or two periods, produce different networks?
`compare_networks()` in Nestimate (Saqr, López-Pernas, & Misiejuk, 2026)
compares two or more networks edge by edge, node by node and on global
metrics, and returns one object from which every table and plot is drawn.
By default the comparison is descriptive; `test` adds a permutation test,
a Bayesian comparison or a bootstrap of the network structure.

| Table | Verb |
|-------|------|
| One row per pair of networks | `summary()` |
| One row per pair and edge | `edge_differences()` |
| One row per pair, node and centrality measure | `node_differences()` |
| One row per pair and global metric | `global_differences()` |
| One row per network and structural metric | `network_metrics()` |

## Data

`group_regulation_long` records the regulation actions of 2,000 students
working in 200 teams of 10, generated synthetically from the
`group_regulation` data of the tna package (Tikka, López-Pernas, & Saqr,
2025). Achievement (`Achiever`, High or Low) is recorded per team.
`build_network()` with `group = "Achiever"` estimates one transition
network per level.

```{r data}
library(Nestimate)
achievers <- build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "relative",
                           actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
                           time = "Time", group = "Achiever")
achievers
```

## Describing the difference

```{r describe}
comparison <- compare_networks(achievers)
comparison
summary(comparison)
```

The comparison takes the difference High minus Low for each of the 81
cells of the weight matrices, self-loops included. 78 cells differ; High
is higher in 51% of them and Low in 46%. The mean absolute difference is
0.03 and the largest, `discuss` to `consensus`, 0.21. The two networks are
alike overall: the edge weights correlate at 0.92 (Pearson and Spearman),
the cosine similarity is 0.95, and the Jaccard similarity of the edges
present in each network is 0.75.

```{r global}
global_differences(comparison)
```

`global_differences()` reports 22 metrics in five groups: deviations of
the weights (mean, median, root mean square and largest absolute
difference), correlations, dissimilarities (Euclidean, Manhattan,
Canberra, Bray-Curtis, Frobenius), similarities (cosine, Jaccard, Dice,
overlap and the RV coefficient, a correlation between matrices; Robert &
Escoufier, 1976), and the agreement of the ranks and signs of the
weights.

```{r global-plot, fig.height = 7}
plot(comparison, type = "global")
```

Each panel is one group of metrics, with a dotted line at the value of
identical networks: 1 for correlations and similarities, 0 for
deviations and dissimilarities.

```{r metrics}
network_metrics(comparison)
```

`network_metrics()` describes each network on its own. Both are almost
complete (76 and 75 of 81 possible edges, density 1 rounded), and their
in-strengths are spread more widely in High (SD 0.91) than in Low (0.72).

### Edges

```{r edges}
head(edge_differences(comparison), 8)
```

`edge_differences()` gives one row per cell: the two weights, their
difference, its absolute value, the relative difference
(`|a - b| / (|a| + |b|)`), the ratio, the ranks of the edge in each
network, `status` (present in both networks, in one, or in neither) and
`higher`, the network in which the edge is larger. `adapt` to `coregulate`
exists only in Low (0 against 0.03).

```{r edges-plot}
plot(comparison, type = "edges")
```

The edge view draws the 20 largest differences as a line between the two
weights, a diamond for High and a square for Low. The line is solid blue
where High is higher and dashed red where Low is higher, and is labelled
with the difference. `discuss` to `consensus` (0.42 in High, 0.21 in Low) and
`synthesis` to `consensus` (0.58 against 0.39) are the largest differences
in favour of High, and `synthesis` to `adapt` (0.14 against 0.30) in
favour of Low.

```{r networks-plot}
plot(comparison, type = "networks")
```

```{r difference-plot}
plot(comparison, type = "difference")
```

The networks view draws each network once; the difference view draws the
signed difference network, blue for transitions stronger in High and red
for transitions stronger in Low.

```{r heatmap-plot}
plot(comparison, type = "heatmap")
```

```{r scatter-plot}
plot(comparison, type = "scatter")
```

The heatmap prints every cell of the difference matrix. The scatter plot
sets each transition's weight in High against its weight in Low; points on
the diagonal are equal in both.

### Nodes

```{r nodes}
node_differences(comparison, measure = "InStrength")
```

`node_differences()` compares the centralities of each state, by default
in-strength, out-strength and betweenness. `consensus` receives the most
in both networks, more in High (2.95 against 2.42), and `adapt` and
`coregulate` receive more in Low.

```{r nodes-plot}
plot(comparison, type = "nodes")
```

## Permutation test

The descriptive tables show where the networks differ, not whether a
difference is larger than sampling would produce. `test = "permutation"`
reassigns the sequences to the two groups 1,000 times, re-estimates both
networks each time, and compares the observed difference of each edge and
node measure with the reassigned ones (Saqr et al., 2025). Two global
statistics test whether the networks differ at all: M, the sum of the
absolute differences over all cells, and S, the largest.

```{r permutation}
tested <- compare_networks(achievers, test = "permutation", iter = 1000,
                           seed = 1)
summary(tested)
```

42 of the 78 transitions and 16 of the 27 node measures differ at the 5%
level, and both global statistics are significant (M = 2.61, S = 0.21,
p = 0.001, the smallest p-value 1,000 permutations can give). `adjust`
corrects the edge p-values for multiple testing, for example
`adjust = "BH"`.

```{r inference-plot, fig.height = 7}
plot(tested, type = "inference")
```

The inference view draws each edge difference as a bar from zero, with its
p-value on the right; a filled marker is significant at 0.05.

## Differences in centralities

`measures = "all"` compares nine centralities. In- and out-strength are
the sums of a state's incoming and outgoing transition probabilities
(Opsahl, Agneessens, & Skvoretz, 2010). Closeness is the inverse of the
summed shortest-path distances to a state (`ClosenessIn`), from it
(`ClosenessOut`) or ignoring direction (`Closeness`), and betweenness the
number of shortest paths that pass through it (Freeman, 1978); a heavier
edge is a shorter step. `BetweennessRSP` counts randomised shortest paths,
which include routes slightly longer than the shortest (Kivimäki et al.,
2016). `Diffusion` sums the weights of the walks of up to n steps that
start at a state (Banerjee et al., 2013), and `Clustering` is the weighted
clustering coefficient (Onnela et al., 2005). The permutation test gives
each a p-value.

```{r centralities}
centralities <- compare_networks(achievers, measures = "all",
                                 test = "permutation", iter = 1000, seed = 1)
summary(centralities)
```

55 of the 81 node measures (nine states, nine measures) differ at the 5%
level: all nine closeness values, eight each for randomised-shortest-path
betweenness and clustering, seven each for in-strength and in-closeness,
five each for out-strength and diffusion, four for betweenness and two for
out-closeness.

```{r betweenness}
node_differences(centralities, measure = "Betweenness")
```

`consensus` lies on most shortest paths in both networks, more in High
(30 against 25, p = 0.001). `synthesis` lies on 7 shortest paths in High
and none in Low (p = 0.003), and `emotion` on 5 against 3 (p = 0.001);
`adapt` lies on more in Low (4 against 1, p = 0.001). `coregulate`,
`discuss` and `plan` differ by 2 or 3 paths without significance.

```{r betweenness-rsp}
node_differences(centralities, measure = "BetweennessRSP")
```

Counting near-shortest routes as well, every state except `adapt` lies on
more routes in High, and all eight differences are significant;
`consensus` has 121 against 88.

```{r closeness}
node_differences(centralities, measure = "Closeness", digits = 3)
```

Closeness is higher in High for every state except `coregulate`.

```{r centralities-plot, fig.height = 8}
plot(centralities, type = "nodes",
     measure = c("Betweenness", "BetweennessRSP", "Closeness", "Diffusion"))
```

The node view draws each state's value in both networks, a diamond for
High and a square for Low, joined by a solid blue line where High is higher
and a dashed red line where Low is higher; stars mark the significant
differences.

## Edge betweenness

Betweenness can also be computed for edges: the number of shortest paths
between states that pass through an edge (Girvan & Newman, 2002). An edge
with a high value carries many of the routes through the network.
`net_edge_betweenness()` returns one network per group whose weights are
these counts, and `permutation()` tests the difference of every edge: it
reassigns the sequences between the groups, re-estimates both transition
networks and recomputes their edge betweenness each time.

```{r edge-betweenness}
edge_betweenness <- net_edge_betweenness(achievers)
edge_betweenness
routes <- permutation(edge_betweenness, iter = 1000, seed = 1)
routes
subset(summary(routes), sig)
```

Shortest paths run over 24 edges in High and 29 in Low, and 10 of the 29
edges tested differ in the number of paths they carry. In Low, 9 shortest
paths pass through `discuss` to `adapt` and none in High; in High,
`discuss` to `synthesis` carries 15 against 8 and `synthesis` to `adapt`
9 against 3.

```{r edge-betweenness-plot}
library(cograph)
splot(routes, edge_positive_color = "#4A6FE3",
      edge_negative_color = "#D33F6A")
```

cograph draws the edges that differ, blue where High carries more paths
and red where Low does.

`bayes_compare()` is the Bayesian route. Edge betweenness is not a simple
function of single transition probabilities, so it draws whole transition
matrices from the Dirichlet posterior of each network, with the Jeffreys
prior added to the counts, and recomputes edge betweenness on every one of
10,000 draws. `diff` is the posterior mean difference in the number of
shortest paths, with its 95% credible interval; an edge is credibly
different when the interval excludes zero.

```{r edge-betweenness-bayes}
routes_posterior <- bayes_compare(edge_betweenness, seed = 1)
routes_posterior
head(summary(routes_posterior), 8)
```

2 of the 78 edges are credibly different: `discuss` to `consensus` carries
2.9 more shortest paths in High (95% interval 1 to 4), and `coregulate` to
`consensus` carries one path in Low and almost none in High. Betweenness
counts whole paths, so its posterior intervals run between whole numbers
and are wide. `discuss` to `adapt`, which carries 7.1 paths in Low and none
in High on average, has an interval from −9 to 0: every draw has it lower
in High (`p_difference` = 1), but the interval reaches zero, so it is not
credibly different. The permutation test found 10 edges, the Bayesian
comparison 2; the two answer the question in different ways, by
reassigning whole sequences and by drawing transition probabilities
independently.

```{r edge-betweenness-bayes-plot}
plot(routes_posterior)
```

## Bayesian comparison

`test = "bayes"` models the transitions out of each state with a Dirichlet
posterior in each network, with the Jeffreys prior of 0.5 added to every
count (Jeffreys, 1946; Johnston & Jendoubi, 2026), and draws the
difference of every edge from the two posteriors (Gelman et al., 2013).
It reports the posterior mean difference, its 95% credible interval and
the probability of direction, the posterior probability that the
difference has the sign of its mean (Makowski et al., 2019). `bayes_p` is
`2 * (1 - pd)`, a two-sided p-value equivalent.

```{r bayes}
bayesian <- compare_networks(achievers, test = "bayes", iter = 1000,
                             seed = 1)
summary(bayesian)
```

39 transitions have a 95% credible interval that excludes zero, against
42 significant in the permutation test; the two agree on 76 of the 81
cells. The posterior treats the transitions as independent counts, while
the permutation test reassigns whole sequences.

```{r bayes-plot, fig.height = 7}
plot(bayesian, type = "inference")
```

### Practical equivalence

A credible interval that excludes zero says the difference is not zero,
not that it is large enough to matter. `rope` sets a region of practical
equivalence around zero on the difference scale (Kruschke, 2018); here a
difference of up to 0.02 in a transition probability is treated as
negligible. Each edge is classed as `different` when its 95% credible
interval lies entirely outside the region, `equivalent` when it lies
entirely inside, and `undecided` otherwise.

```{r rope}
equivalence <- compare_networks(achievers, test = "bayes", iter = 1000,
                                seed = 1, rope = 0.02)
subset(edge_differences(equivalence), bayes_decision == "different")
```

19 transitions are different, 22 practically equivalent and 40
undecided. The different ones include the largest differences of the
descriptive comparison, such as `discuss` to `consensus` and `synthesis`
to `adapt`.

### `bayes_compare()`

`bayes_compare()` runs the same model on its own, with 10,000 posterior
draws by default. An edge is credibly different when its 95% interval
excludes zero, its posterior mean difference exceeds 0.01 in absolute
value, and the interval bound nearest zero exceeds 0.001.

```{r bayes-compare}
posterior <- bayes_compare(achievers, seed = 1)
head(summary(posterior), 8)
```

The table gives each transition's weight and count in both networks, the
posterior mean difference, an effect size (the difference divided by its
posterior standard deviation), the credible interval and the probability
that the difference has the sign of its mean (`p_difference`). 38
transitions are credibly different. `adapt` to `coregulate` occurs 11
times in Low and never in High; its interval, [−0.049, −0.008], excludes
zero.

```{r bayes-compare-plot, fig.height = 7}
plot(posterior)
```

The plot draws the credibly different transitions as a difference
network, blue where High is higher and red where Low is higher, each edge
labelled with its posterior mean difference and credible interval.

## Bootstrap of the structure

`test = "bootstrap"` resamples the nodes of each network (Snijders &
Borgatti, 1999; Davison & Hinkley, 1997) and compares four structural
measures: density, mean weight, centralization and reciprocity. It reads
only the weight matrices, so it also works for matrices without data.

```{r bootstrap}
structural <- compare_networks(achievers, test = "bootstrap", iter = 1000,
                               seed = 1)
subset(global_differences(structural), category == "Structure (bootstrap)")
```

None of the four measures differs (p between 0.69 and 0.99): the two
networks have the same overall structure, and they differ in which
transitions carry the weight.

## Accounting for nesting

Students are nested in teams, and the achievement level is given per
team. With `actor = "Group"`, the permutation test reassigns whole teams
instead of single students, and `global_differences()` gains three
`Nesting` rows.

```{r nested}
nested <- compare_networks(achievers, test = "permutation", iter = 1000,
                           seed = 1, actor = "Group")
subset(global_differences(nested, digits = 3),
       category %in% c("Global Test (permutation)", "Nesting"))
```

The intraclass correlation is −0.002, and the design effect is 1.03 for
the transitions and 1.20 for M. The networks still differ overall
(M = 2.61, p = 0.001), and 42 transitions remain significant. The
article on nested data describes these quantities.

## More than two networks

`mark_phases()` divides each student's actions into three phases of equal
length, and `build_network()` estimates one network per phase. Every
student contributes to all three phases, so with `actor = "Actor"` the
permutation test reassigns each student's sequences between phases within
the student. `reference = "early"` compares the other two phases with the
first instead of comparing every pair.

```{r phases}
phased <- mark_phases(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", time = "Time",
                      n = 3, labels = c("early", "middle", "late"))
phases <- build_network(phased, method = "relative", actor = "Actor",
                        action = "Action", time = "Time", group = "phase")
over_time <- compare_networks(phases, reference = "early",
                              test = "permutation", iter = 1000, seed = 1,
                              actor = "Actor")
summary(over_time)
```

The three phases are nearly identical: the edge weights correlate at 0.99
with those of the early phase, and the largest difference is 0.08. Neither
global test is significant (p = 0.71 and 0.72 for M). Six and four of the
78 transitions differ at the 5% level, about the four that 78 tests at
that level produce by chance; `adjust = "BH"` corrects the edge p-values
for the number of tests.

```{r phases-plot}
plot(over_time, type = "edges", pair = "late")
```

`pair` selects the comparisons a view or a table shows, by the pair name,
the two network names or one network name.
